newsitem.title: THAILAND: NatWest Securities says reassessing Thai presence.
newsitem.headline: NatWest Securities says reassessing Thai presence.

text.p: NatWest Securities Asia is reassessing its investment options in Thailand after sacking its local research team, the firm's Managing Director Meocre Li told Reuters on Friday.
The firm, part of National Westminster Bank Plc, ultimately wished to take a stake in a Thai securities firm but would progress cautiously towards that goal, he said.
"I think we did not make the progress we would have liked to see in the last two years," he said.
"I think in part it's because the market is very slow and ... I think it wasn't the kind of standard we would like to have largely in terms of the quality of the people that we had," he said.
An array of economic concerns, including slower growth and a high current account deficit, has seen the Thai market lose more than half its value from 1996 highs.
The market's composite SET Index closed on Friday at 684.00, down from a previous year high close of 1415.04 in February 1996.
Wheelock NatWest received approval to open a Thai representative office in October 1995 but recently retrenched its four analysts including its former chief representative officer, Li said.
Wheelock Natwest was absorbed into Natwest Securities Asia late last year and the new firm announced a revamp of its Asian operations in January.
"It is certainly not a withdrawal (from Thailand). We still have the rep office, a couple of corporate finance people and the capital markets side is still there as before," he said.
"I am still in discusion with some local houses on growing closer associations. What it is clear is that because of the slowness of the market in Thailand we are not in a rush," he said.
NatWest Securities Asia still considered Thailand an attractive investment location, he said.
"At the outset when we picked the various countries in terms of their potential Indonesia and Thailand are the two countries among the ASEAN countries considered by us to be top priority," he said.
But the fragile financial situation of some Thai brokers, hit by high financing costs and declining portfolio quality, makes clear identification of opportunities more difficult, he said.
"Actually I think it is a good time to consider what to do and discuss what to do with some local houses ... it is making it more difficult to assess what we can do together," he said.
